title: ZEE Grabbed the FIFA World Cup Rights Ten Days Before Kickoff. It Paid 40% Less Than FIFA Wanted.
excerpt: After JioStar balked at the price, ZEE swooped in at $60 million, launched a new sports network, and bet its future on Indian football fandom.
body:
For months, Indian football fans had one nagging question: who would broadcast the 2026 FIFA World Cup? With the tournament starting on June 11 in North America, the answer arrived almost absurdly late. Zee Entertainment has secured the broadcast rights for 39 FIFA events from 2026 through 2034 — clinching the deal barely ten days before the opening whistle.

The agreement, finalised on June 1, covers not just the 2026 World Cup across the United States, Canada, and Mexico, but also the 2030 World Cup, the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup, and several youth and futsal tournaments. It is the most significant sports broadcasting deal in India this year, and possibly the most dramatic.

## How ZEE Pulled It Off

The backstory matters. FIFA had initially sought roughly $100 million for the Indian broadcast package. Negotiations with the JioStar combine — the merged sports broadcasting behemoth that dominates Indian cricket rights — stalled over valuation disagreements. India, one of the world's fastest-growing football markets, was in danger of becoming one of the last major territories without a confirmed broadcaster.

ZEE stepped in at approximately $60 million, roughly 40 percent below FIFA's opening ask. For a company that exited sports broadcasting eight years ago when it sold its sports assets to Sony, it is a remarkable re-entry. ZEE's stock rose about 7 percent on the news, with the board announcing a meeting on June 10 to consider a fresh fundraise — likely to bankroll the investment.

## Unite8 Sports: A New Brand

To deliver the coverage, ZEE is launching Unite8 Sports, a dedicated network with four linear channels: Unite8 Sports 1 and Unite8 Sports 1 HD in Hindi, and Unite8 Sports 2 and Unite8 Sports 2 HD in English. Digital viewers can stream every match live on ZEE5.

The branding choice is deliberate. The World Cup will feature 48 teams for the first time, played across 16 cities in three countries. ZEE is betting that the expanded format — with more matches, more time zones, and more drama — will pull Indian audiences deeper into football culture.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the estimated 4.5 million Indians and Indian Americans in the United States, the timing is almost poetic. The World Cup is coming to their backyard — matches in New York, Los Angeles, Dallas, Houston, and the Bay Area — and now an Indian broadcaster will carry the coverage with Hindi and English commentary tailored for South Asian audiences.

The opening match kicks off on June 11 in Mexico City. The FIFA World Cup Trophy Tour recently stopped at the American Museum of Natural History in New York — a city now home to an Indian-origin mayor, a growing desi football fanbase, and a World Cup venue across the river in New Jersey.

## ZEE's Bigger Bet

This is not just about football. ZEE's move signals a strategic pivot at a moment when its core entertainment business faces headwinds. The company reported a weak March quarter, and the broader Indian advertising market remains under pressure. Sports rights — especially global ones that JioStar does not control — offer ZEE a differentiated asset.

The 2026 World Cup will test whether Indian audiences tune in at scale. India's national team did not qualify, but that may matter less than it once did. The Indian Super League has grown viewership steadily, Indian fans packed stadiums at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, and social media engagement around European football in India has surged. ZEE is wagering that the market has crossed a tipping point.

If the numbers hold, the 2030 World Cup — which will be partly held in Africa, another region with deep ties to the Indian diaspora — becomes the real payoff. ZEE has eight years to prove the bet was worth it.
